opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a great question, because on the surface the two ideas can look like they're pulling in opposite directions, and I think the interesting stuff happens where they meet.

What excites me about long context in large language models is that it's a glimpse of what becomes possible when a system can bring a rich history of experience to bear on the moment it's in. You see in-context learning: the model isn't updating its weights, but it adapts its behavior based on what it's seen in the conversation so far. That's powerful. It suggests that a lot of what we call "learning" can happen in how a system uses its memory, not only in how it changes its parameters.

From the perspective of the Alberta Plan, though, the thing we care most about is the agent that never stops. It's out in the world, interacting continually, and its experience is a single unbroken stream. That stream doesn't fit in any context window, no matter how long. A prosthetic arm working with a person for years, or a robot in a home: those histories are effectively unbounded. So the question becomes: how do you take that endless stream and turn it into something compact, predictive, and useful right now? That's where incremental, online learning comes in. You're constantly compressing experience into knowledge, into predictions about what will happen next, into a sense of state, rather than just storing everything and hoping to attend to the right piece later.

So, to me, long context and continual learning are complementary. Long histories give you a wonderful short-term, flexible memory. Incremental learning gives you the long-term growth: the agent that becomes more capable, more personalized, more attuned to the specific person or environment it's working with, day after day. What excites me is the prospect of systems that do both. They'd use rich recent context to adapt quickly in the moment, and keep learning from the stream so they aren't frozen at the point their training ended.

And I think that matters a lot for the kinds of applications I care about, like assistive technology and rehabilitation. People change, bodies change, environments change. A system that only has a long memory but can't really grow from it will eventually fall out of step with the person it's meant to help. A system that learns continually can stay in partnership with them. That's the future I find really compelling.

r001.rationale: The response discusses using a rich conversation history and adapting from it, but does not identify relating information across widely separated parts of a long token history.

r002.rationale: It says the experience stream is unbounded and describes incremental learning as compressing it into knowledge and predictions rather than storing everything.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and it's one I think about a lot, because on the surface it looks like these two things are pulling in opposite directions. A lot of the work we've been doing with the Alberta Plan is really about the opposite of long histories, in a sense. It's about an agent that learns continually, online, from a stream of experience, where it can't just go back and reread everything that ever happened to it. It has to compress what it's seen into something compact, into predictions and features and a representation it carries forward, and then update that on every single time step.

So when I look at large language models getting access to these very long contexts, hundreds of thousands or millions of tokens, what excites me isn't actually the length itself. What excites me is that it puts a really sharp question on the table about what history is for. Because the naive view is, more history is just better, you remember more, so you do better. But if you think about it from the perspective of an animal, or a person, or one of our learning agents, we don't work that way at all. I don't carry around a verbatim transcript of my last twenty years. I carry around a very lossy, very selective summary that's been shaped by what mattered to me, by what I needed to predict, by what was surprising. And that compression isn't a bug. That's the intelligence.

So the thing I find exciting is that we now have a system that can, in principle, look at the full raw stream, and that lets us ask, empirically, what parts of that stream actually matter. What does a system need to pull out of a long history in order to act well right now? And that's exactly the question that temporal difference learning and general value functions are asking from the other side. They're saying, don't store the history, store predictions about the future that summarize what the history told you. And I think there's a really interesting convergence coming where these long-context systems start to behave less like a searchable archive and more like a continually adapting agent, where the context is doing the work that our learned state representations do.

The other piece, and this is where my own interests really light up, is in the assistive technology and human-machine partnership side of things. If you have a prosthetic limb, or any device that's working alongside a person for years, the history that matters is deeply personal and deeply nonstationary. The person changes, their body changes, their goals change. And a system that can hold and adapt to a long shared history with one specific person, rather than being frozen at deployment, that starts to look like something we could genuinely call a partner. That's what I've wanted for a long time. So I'm less excited about long context as a capability and more excited about it as a step toward machines that actually have a life history with the people they're working with, and that keep learning from it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses long contexts and examining what parts of a history matter, but does not identify relating information across widely separated parts of the token history as what excites Pilarski.

r002.rationale: It says Alberta Plan agents learn online from a stream and cannot reread everything that happened, so they compress experience into a compact representation instead of retaining the full history.

astra-6.text:
What excites me is the possibility of connecting what a system is doing right now to a much longer history of interaction. In incremental learning, the question is how each new experience helps you become better at predicting and acting. A long history gives you more material to work with: you can revisit something that happened earlier, recognize that it matters now, and use it to inform your next decision.

But having access to a history isn’t quite the same as learning from it. The interesting question is how you turn that experience into knowledge that remains useful as the world changes. What do you retain? What do you update? What can you compress into a prediction rather than having to read the whole history again?

That’s where I see a connection to the Alberta Plan: moving toward systems that learn continually through interaction. I’m excited by the possibility of an assistant whose relationship with you develops over time—one that uses shared experience to anticipate what would be helpful, and then learns from whether its help actually worked.

r001.rationale: It describes connecting current activity to a much longer history, revisiting earlier events, and recognizing when they matter now.

r002.rationale: It discusses what to retain and compress, but does not state that incremental learning is intended to avoid retaining histories of past samples.

sol-6.1.text:
What excites me is the possibility of continuity. An interaction doesn’t have to start from scratch every time. A system can draw on a history of what you’ve done together, what mattered to you, and how those things have changed.

From the perspective of incremental learning and the Alberta Plan, though, I’d distinguish having access to a long history from learning continually from experience. They’re related, but they aren’t the same thing. The interesting question is how that history helps a system make better predictions, adapt its behavior, and become more useful through ongoing interaction.

Imagine an assistant that works with you over years. It could learn when to offer help, when to stay quiet, and how to support goals that evolve over time. That prospect of a system getting better through a shared lifetime of experience is what I find really exciting.
